entries.test: Whether OpenAI's inference spend in CY2024 (reported here as $3.77B) and H1 CY2025 ($5.02B) was higher than its reported revenue of $3.7B and $4.3B for those periods.
entries.note: For CY2024 the gap is small ($3.77B vs $3.7B), so 'easily eclipsed' is an overstatement for that year. 'It seems' is a mild hedge on an inference drawn from figures.

entries.test: Whether OpenAI's actual inference spend (e.g. Azure inference for CY2024 and H1 CY2025) was much higher than the publicly reported $2B and $2.5B.
entries.note: The normalised proposition is framed as Zitron's belief, which makes it a claim about his mind. The claim he actually makes is about OpenAI's spending versus what was reported.

entries.test: Whether OpenAI's Azure inference spend from January through September 2025 was about $8.67B, close to or above the reported $9B full-year cash burn.
entries.note: The checkable core is the $8.67B figure and how it conflicts with the $9B burn projection. 'Cannot reconcile' is his framing.

entries.test: Whether OpenAI's reported CY2025 revenue reached $13 billion or more.
entries.note: 'Cannot see a path' reads as a firm expectation that OpenAI will miss $13B. The deadline (end of 2025) has passed.

entries.test: Whether the figures in the documents (e.g. $3.77B inference in 2024, implied revenue of at least $2.47B) differ materially from contemporaneous press reports (e.g. $2B inference, $3.7B revenue).
entries.note: The 'makes me wonder' clause commits to nothing. Only the 'materially different' part can be graded.
This is a conditional either/or about how much third parties pay, followed by speculation ('wonder whether... could'). Readers would not agree on a single test for it.
